stem: After `POST /v1/orders` creates an order, which response header gives the address of the new order?
explanation: A `201 Created` reply carries `Location` with the address of the new resource. `Content-Type` names the format of a body, `Authorization` carries credentials, and `Retry-After` tells a client how long to wait before trying again.

stem: A `POST /v1/reports` starts a long export. The service replies `202 Accepted` and a `Location` header that points to a status page. What does the reply tell the client?

options.text: It was accepted but is not finished yet
It finished and its file is in the reply body
It was refused because the report already exists
It will be repeated automatically after a short delay

explanation: `202 Accepted` means the work was queued, and the status page is where the client checks progress. A finished export would be a `200` or `201` with the result, a duplicate would be a `409`, and the server does not schedule repeats on its own.

stem: A script sends `GET /v1/orders/9981` and receives `404 Not Found`. What does this mean?

options.text: The token in the request has expired
The server ran out of memory while handling it
The `GET` method is not supported on that path
The server has no resource at that path

explanation: `404` says nothing exists at the requested path. An expired token gives `401`, a server fault gives a `5XX` code, and an unsupported method gives `405`.

stem:
A deployment script runs this command and the service replies `415 Unsupported Media Type`.
```bash
curl -X POST https://api.example.internal/v1/tickets \
  -H "Content-Type: text/plain" \
  -d '{"title":"disk full"}'
```
Which change fixes the request?
explanation: The body is JSON but the `Content-Type` header says plain text, so the service refuses the media type. Changing the method or adding `Accept` leaves the mismatch in place, and `Retry-After` is a response header.

stem: A client times out and sends the identical `PUT /v1/users/42` request three times. What is the state of user 42 afterwards?

options.text: The same as after the first request that arrived
Three copies of the user exist under new addresses
The second request undoes the first one
The user is locked until an administrator resets it

explanation: `PUT` is idempotent: it replaces the resource at one address with the supplied body, so repeats leave the same state. It does not create copies, toggle the result, or lock anything.

stem: A script calls a protected endpoint without any `Authorization` header. Which status does a well-built service return?
explanation: `401` means credentials are missing or not valid. `403` is for a known identity that lacks permission, `404` means no such resource, and `405` says the method is not supported on that path.

stem: A service account with a read-only scope sends a valid token on `DELETE /v1/orders/1042` and gets `403 Forbidden`. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The token is missing or has expired
The caller is known but lacks permission
The order does not exist on the server
The server cannot reach its order database

explanation: `403` means the request was understood and the caller was identified, but the action is not allowed. A missing or expired token gives `401`, a missing order gives `404`, and an unreachable database gives a `5XX` code.

stem: A monitoring script receives `502`, `503` and `504` replies from an API. Which status class do all three belong to?
explanation: Codes from `500` to `599` are server errors. `2XX` is success, `3XX` tells the client to look elsewhere, and `4XX` blames the request.

stem: A script posts a JSON body that is missing its closing brace. Which status best reports the problem?
explanation: A body that cannot be parsed is a malformed request, which is `400`. `413` is for a body over the size limit, `405` means the method is not supported on the path, and `503` means the service cannot take requests right now.

stem: A `POST /v1/users` tries to register an email address that already belongs to another user. Which status best reports the problem?
explanation: `409` signals that the request clashes with the current state of the resource set. `401` is about credentials, `405` would mean `POST` is not supported on the path, and `503` is a temporary service fault.

stem: `DELETE /v1/reports` returns `405 Method Not Allowed` with the header `Allow: GET, POST`. What should the client conclude?

options.text: The path does not exist on this server
The path exists but does not support `DELETE`
The token lacks permission for that path
The server is busy and will accept `DELETE` later

explanation: `405` plus `Allow` lists the methods the path does support. A missing path is `404`, a permission problem is `403`, and a busy server returns `503`.

stem: An automation job gets `429 Too Many Requests` with `Retry-After: 30`. What should the job do next?

options.text: Repeat the request at once with a fresh token
Change the method to `PUT` to bypass the limit
Stop and mark the order as permanently invalid
Wait about 30 seconds, then repeat the request

explanation: `Retry-After` states how long to pause before another attempt, so the job waits and retries. Hammering the endpoint or changing method does not lift a rate limit, and the order itself is not at fault. A fresh token does not lift a rate limit either.

stem: A gateway returns `504 Gateway Timeout` for `GET /v1/orders`. Which statement fits?

options.text: The client sent a body that is too large
The token was accepted but lacks the needed scope
The upstream service did not reply in time
The path was moved to a new address

explanation: `504` comes from an intermediary that waited too long for an upstream reply. An oversized body gives `413`, a scope problem gives `403`, and a moved path gives a `3XX` code.

stem:
```bash
$ curl http://api.example.internal/v1/orders/7
$ curl -i http://api.example.internal/v1/orders/7
HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Location: https://api.example.internal/v1/orders/7
```
The first command prints nothing, because the redirect reply has an empty body. Which change makes `curl` print the order?

options.text: Add `-X GET` to force the method
Add `-I` so only headers are requested
Add `-k` to skip certificate checks on the connection

explanation: By default `curl` does not follow a `301`, so it shows the empty redirect body. `-L` follows `Location` to the new address. The method is already `GET`, `-I` asks for headers only, and `-k` concerns certificates, not redirects.

stem: A client sends `GET /v1/config` with `If-None-Match: "v7"` and receives `304 Not Modified`. What should the client do?

options.text: Retry with `If-Match` to force a refresh
Keep its cached copy, as no body was sent
Follow the `Location` header to a new address

explanation: `304` tells the client its stored version still matches the server's `ETag`, so it reuses the cache. It does not mean the resource moved or was removed, and `If-Match` is for conditional writes.

stem: Two engineers read a ticket and both get `ETag: "a1"`; the first sends `PUT /v1/tickets/55` with `If-Match: "a1"` and succeeds, so the ticket now has the tag `"a2"`. The second sends the same request with `If-Match: "a1"`. Which status does the service return?
explanation: The second `If-Match` no longer matches the current tag, so the condition fails and the service refuses the write with `412`. `428` applies when a client omits the condition, `304` answers conditional reads, and the credentials were never the problem.

stem: A client sends `DELETE /v1/sessions/ab12` and gets `204 No Content`. What does the reply contain besides headers?

options.text: Nothing, because the body is empty
A JSON copy of the deleted session
A link to the next page of sessions

explanation: `204` means success with no body, so there is nothing to parse after the headers. A reply that returns the deleted record or a message would use a `200` instead, and a link to a next page belongs to a list reply.

stem: A script runs `DELETE /v1/sessions/abc` twice. The first call returns `204` and the second returns `404`. Is `DELETE` still idempotent?

options.text: No, because the second status proves the call changed state
No, because the RFC lists `DELETE` as not idempotent
Yes, because the server ends in the same state either way
Yes, because the server must return `204` again on the repeat

explanation: Idempotency is about the effect on the server, not the status code: after one or many calls the session is gone. The RFC lists `DELETE` as idempotent, and nothing requires the repeat to return the same code.

stem: Where should a script place a bearer token when it calls `GET /v1/orders`?
explanation: Bearer tokens travel in `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. `Content-Type` and `Accept` describe formats, and `Location` is a response header that a client cannot send.

stem: A script must call an endpoint that expects a username and password. Which `curl` option supplies them as `user:password`?
explanation: `-u` builds a `Basic` `Authorization` header from the pair. `-d` sets a request body, `-o` names an output file, and `-X` sets the method.

stem: An engineer wants only the response headers of `https://api.example.internal/v1/ping`, without downloading the body. Which command does that?
explanation: `-I` sends a `HEAD` request, so only headers come back. `-i` prints headers followed by the body, `-s` hides the progress meter but still prints the body, and `-L` follows redirects.

stem: A pipeline step runs `curl -s https://api.example.internal/v1/health`. The service returns `503`, yet the step passes. Which option makes `curl` exit with an error on a `4XX` or `5XX` reply?
explanation: `curl` exits with success whenever it receives any reply unless `--fail` (`-f`) turns `400` and above into a failing exit code. `--include` only adds the headers to the output, `--location` follows redirects, and `--insecure` skips certificate checks.

stem: Which command saves the reply from `https://api.example.internal/v1/report` to a file named `report.json`?
explanation: A capital `-O` names the output document. A lowercase `-o` writes the progress log to that file, `-P` sets a directory prefix, and `-q` just silences output while treating the name as another address.

stem: In the standard `wget` on most Linux hosts, which option adds a custom request header such as `Accept: application/json`?
explanation: `--header` sends an extra header with the request. In `wget`, `-H` means span hosts when recursing, `-A` sets a list of accepted file suffixes, and `--post-data` sends the text as a request body.

stem: A team keeps one Postman collection and wants to run its requests against both the staging and production hosts by changing one setting at run time. What should hold the host name?

options.text: A fixed host typed into every request
A separate collection for each host
A header named `Host-Name` on each request

explanation: Environments store named variables, so one collection can use `{{base_url}}` and pick staging or production at run time. Hard-coded hosts and duplicate collections must be edited together, and a custom header does not change where the request goes.

stem: In Postman, what is a collection?

options.text: A saved group of related requests that can be run together
A named set of variables for one deployment target
A history of the status codes that a server has returned to the app
A server that stores responses for later replay

explanation: A collection bundles saved requests, optionally with folders and tests. The set of variables for a target is an environment, and Postman is a client tool that does not store server responses for replay.

stem: An API retired `POST /v1/orders` in favor of a new address and wants every client to resend the same method and body there. Which status fits best?
explanation: `308` is permanent and requires the client to repeat the same method and body. `301` and `302` allow a client to switch `POST` to `GET`, and `307` keeps the method but is temporary.

stem: A payment client retries `POST /v1/charges` after a timeout, and a customer is charged twice. Which design makes the retry safe?

options.text: Resend the request as `GET` so repeats are harmless
Add a `Retry-After` header to the request
Send a unique idempotency key the service uses to detect repeats
Compress the body so the request finishes sooner

explanation: `POST` is not idempotent by default, so the client attaches a unique key and the service returns the first result for any repeat. `GET` cannot create a charge, `Retry-After` is a response header, and compression does not stop duplicates.

stem: Only the `email` field of profile 7 must change, and the other fields must stay as they are. Which request fits best?

options.text: `PATCH /v1/profiles/7` with a body that holds just `email`
`PUT /v1/profiles/7` with a body that holds just the `email` field
`POST /v1/profiles` with a body that holds just `email`

explanation: `PATCH` applies a partial change to the resource. `PUT` replaces the whole resource, so omitted fields would be lost, `POST` to the collection creates a new profile, and `DELETE` removes the profile.

stem: A script must add a new order to the collection and let the server choose the order number. Which request fits?

options.text: `PUT /v1/orders` with the order in the body
`POST /v1/orders` with the order in the body
`GET /v1/orders` with the order in the query
`DELETE /v1/orders` with the order in the body

explanation: `POST` to a collection creates a new member and lets the server assign its address. `PUT` needs the full address of the target, `GET` only reads, and `DELETE` removes.

stem: A retry wrapper may resend a request after a network timeout. Which THREE methods are idempotent, so resending is safe by definition?
explanation: `GET`, `PUT` and `DELETE` are idempotent, so repeating them leaves the server in the same state. `POST` and `PATCH` are not idempotent by default, because each call can create or change something again.

stem: A script sends a JSON body and wants JSON back. Which TWO request headers does it set?
explanation: `Content-Type` describes the body being sent and `Accept` states the reply format the client wants. `Location`, `Retry-After` and `ETag` are headers that a server sends in replies.

stem: Which TWO replies are client errors (4XX)?
explanation: `404` and `409` both fall in the 400 range, which blames the request. `502` and `503` are server-side errors, and `304` is a redirection-class code that means the cached copy is still valid.

stem: An update must be applied only if the resource is unchanged since the client read it. Which TWO headers make that check possible?
explanation: The server labels each version with `ETag`, and the client sends that label back in `If-Match` so a stale write is refused. `Accept` picks a format, `Retry-After` sets a delay, and `Location` gives an address.

stem: Which TWO Postman features support running the same requests against different hosts without editing each request?

options.text: A collection that groups the saved requests
A host name hard-coded in each request address
An environment that holds variables such as a base URL
A duplicate of each request for every host
Saved response examples attached to a request

explanation: A collection keeps the requests together, and an environment supplies variables such as the base URL. Hard-coded hosts and duplicated requests must be edited one by one, and response examples document replies but do not change the target.

stem: Which TWO status codes are temporary redirects?
explanation: `302` and `307` tell a client to use another address this time while keeping the original address valid. `301` and `308` are permanent, and `304` is not a redirect at all.

stem: Manage order records on the orders API. Use the notes and help text shown, then type each command. Replies are not shown because nothing is run.

output: Bodies are JSON. A request with a body must say so in a Content-Type header.
The server picks the number of a new order. PATCH changes only the fields sent.
-i, --include            print response headers before the body

steps.label: Type the command that creates an order with the body {"sku":"A-100","qty":2}
Type the command that reads order 1042; no body or extra header is needed
Type the command that changes only the quantity of order 1042 to 5, with the body {"qty":5}
Type the command that removes order 1042
Order 1042 is now deleted. Choose the status a later read of it returns

options.text: 204 No Content, because the order is empty
301 Moved Permanently, to an archive address
404 Not Found, because the order is gone
401 Unauthorized, because the owner is gone

explanation: A new order is created with a POST to the collection and a JSON body that carries a Content-Type header. A read needs only the address, a PATCH changes just the fields it sends, and a DELETE targets the single order. A later read of a deleted order finds nothing at that address.

partExplanations.create: POST to the collection with the JSON header and body; curl also infers POST from the body.
partExplanations.read: A plain curl with the order address performs a GET.
partExplanations.update: PATCH to the single order with just the quantity, so other fields stay as they are.
partExplanations.delete: DELETE to the single order address.
partExplanations.after: Nothing exists at the address any more, so the service answers 404.

stem: Complete the requests that manage orders on the orders API. New orders get their number from the server, bodies are JSON, and a delete reply carries no body.

fields.label: Method that adds a new order to the collection
Header that tells the server the create body is JSON
Method that changes only the quantity of order 1042
Header that makes the update fail if another client changed the order after it was read
Status of a successful delete with no reply body

explanation: A POST to the collection lets the server choose the number, and Content-Type declares the JSON body. PATCH changes part of an order, If-Match carries the tag from the earlier read so a stale write fails, and a delete with nothing to return uses 204.

partExplanations.create: POST creates a member of the collection; PUT needs the full address and GET only reads.
partExplanations.ctype: Content-Type describes the request body; Accept describes the reply wanted.
partExplanations.update: PATCH sends a partial change, while POST creates and DELETE removes.
partExplanations.guard: If-Match makes the write conditional on the tag read earlier.
partExplanations.delete: 204 means success with no body; 201 is for creation and 304 for cached reads.

stem: A client creates a support ticket, revises it, and removes it. Put the requests in the order the client sends them. Rules: the client needs the address from the create reply before it can touch the ticket; the tag from a read must be in hand before a conditional update is sent; the revised content is confirmed before the ticket is removed; the check for a missing ticket comes after the removal.

steps.text: Send a DELETE to the ticket address; the service replies 204 No Content
Send a GET to the ticket address and note the ETag in the reply
Send a GET to the ticket address and receive 404 Not Found
Send a GET to the ticket address to confirm the revised content is stored
Send a POST with the ticket as JSON; the service replies 201 Created with a Location header
Send a PUT to the ticket address with the revised ticket and an If-Match header holding that tag

explanation: The create reply supplies the address, a read supplies the tag, the conditional update uses it, a second read confirms the new content, the delete removes the ticket, and a final read shows it is gone.

partExplanations.0: The create comes first because its Location header gives the ticket address.
partExplanations.1: The first read returns the ETag that the update needs.
partExplanations.2: The conditional update sends that ETag in If-Match.
partExplanations.3: The confirming read follows the update and precedes the removal.
partExplanations.4: The delete removes the ticket after the content was confirmed.
partExplanations.5: The closing read shows 404 because the ticket no longer exists.

stem: A script logged these ten calls against the orders API. Use the table to answer each question.

fields.label: How many calls failed with a client error (4XX)?
How many calls failed with a server error (5XX)?
Which call tells the client how long to wait before trying again?

explanation: Rows 1, 3, 6 and 10 returned a 2XX code, which makes four. Rows 2, 7 and 9 returned 415, 429 and 404, which makes three client errors. Rows 4 and 8 returned 502 and 503, which makes two server errors. Row 5 is the only 3XX reply, and row 7 carries the Retry-After note.

partExplanations.ok: Statuses 200, 200, 201 and 201 in rows 1, 3, 6 and 10 give 4.
partExplanations.redirect: Row 5 returned 301, the only 3XX code in the log.
partExplanations.wait: Row 7 has Retry-After: 30, which gives the delay.

stem: In this design the gateway checks tokens and the orders service owns the order data. Place the best element for each need named below the request path.

zones.name: Sends Accept and reads Location after a 201
Rejects a request with no token using 401
Returns 404 for an order number that does not exist
Holds the order record that a 201 reports

explanation: The client script builds the request and reads the reply headers. The gateway authenticates and returns 401 before the service sees the call, the orders service knows which orders exist and returns 404, and the database holds the stored order. A static file server and a message queue play no part in this request path.

partExplanations.z1: The client sends Accept and uses the Location header from the reply.
partExplanations.z2: The gateway checks tokens, so a missing token ends there with 401.
partExplanations.z3: The service owns the order data, so it decides that an order does not exist.
partExplanations.z4: The database stores the order record behind the service.

stem: A script sent a request to create an order and it failed. The raw reply is shown line by line. Select the two lines that explain why the call failed and when the client may try again.
explanation: The status line shows 429, so the service refused the call because of the request rate, and Retry-After says to wait 30 seconds. The format, length, server name and request tag describe the reply but do not explain the failure.

partExplanations.status: The 429 status explains why the call failed.
partExplanations.ctype: Content-Type only names the reply format.
partExplanations.clen: Content-Length only gives the size of the reply body.
partExplanations.retry: Retry-After gives the number of seconds to wait before another attempt.
partExplanations.server: The Server header names the machine that replied and says nothing about the failure.
partExplanations.reqid: The request tag helps support find the call in logs but does not explain it.

stem: Match each status code to the meaning a client should take from it.

choices.text: A new resource exists and its address is in the Location header
The cached copy is still current, so no body was sent
The request clashes with the current state of the resource
The call worked and there is nothing to return
The service cannot take requests right now
The credentials are missing or were not accepted
The resource moved permanently to a new address

explanation: Each code carries a distinct meaning: 201 reports a creation, 204 a success with no body, 304 a still-valid cache, 401 a credentials problem, 409 a state clash and 503 a temporary service fault. The permanent move belongs to 301 and 308.

partExplanations.p1: 201 reports a creation and points to the new resource with Location.
partExplanations.p2: 204 is success with an empty body.
partExplanations.p3: 304 answers a conditional read when the stored copy still matches.
partExplanations.p4: 401 means credentials are missing or not valid.
partExplanations.p5: 409 means the request clashes with the current state.
partExplanations.p6: 503 means the service cannot handle requests at the moment.

stem: Sort each request into the bucket that describes how repeating it behaves under the HTTP rules.

items.text: PUT a full replacement of order 1042
POST a new order to the orders collection
PATCH that appends a note to order 1042
POST that starts a new export job

explanation: GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent, so repeating them leaves the same state. POST normally creates something new on every call, and a PATCH that appends adds another note each time.

partExplanations.i1: A read does not change state, so repeats are harmless.
partExplanations.i2: Replacing a resource with the same content gives the same result every time.
partExplanations.i3: After the first delete the order is gone, and repeats leave that state.
partExplanations.i4: Each POST to a collection creates another order.
partExplanations.i5: Appending adds one more note on each repeat.
partExplanations.i6: Each POST starts another job run.
